before: For the moment had come—that pause when dawn trembles and night holds still, when a single feather dropped into the scale would tip it. One feather, and the house would have sunk and fallen, turning over and pitching down into the depths of darkness. Picnickers would have boiled their kettles in the ruined room; lovers would have taken shelter there, lying on the bare floorboards; the shepherd would have kept his dinner on the bricks, and the tramp would have slept there wrapped in his coat against the cold. Later the roof would have caved in. Briars and hemlock would have smothered path, step and window, growing unevenly but vigorously over the mound, until a trespasser who had strayed off his path could have guessed only from a red-hot poker among the nettles, or a fragment of china in the hemlock, that someone had lived here once; that there had once been a house.

before: Then there was the cook—Mildred, Marian, some name of that kind—a red-haired woman, with a quick temper, as they all have, but kind as well, if you knew how to take her. Many’s the laugh they’d had together. She always kept back a plate of soup for Maggie; sometimes a bit of ham; whatever was going spare. They lived well, back then. They had everything they wanted. (Sitting in the wicker armchair by the nursery fender, with the hot tea inside her, she unwound her ball of memories, easily and merrily.) There was always something going on—people in the house, twenty to stay at a time, sometimes, and washing up going on till well after midnight.

before: Then, truly, peace had come. From the sea to the shore came breaths of peace, messages of it: never again to disturb its sleep, but to lull it into a deeper rest, and to confirm whatever the dreamers dreamed, holily and wisely—what else could it be murmuring?—as Lily Briscoe laid her head on the pillow in the clean, quiet room and listened to the sea. In through the open window came the voice of the world’s beauty, murmuring too softly for its exact words to be made out—but what did that matter, if the meaning was clear? It pleaded with the sleepers (the house was full once more; Mrs. Beckwith was staying, and Mr. Carmichael as well) that if they would not actually come down to the beach, they should at least raise the blind and look out. Then they would see night flowing down in purple, his head crowned, his scepter set with jewels, and how a child might gaze into his eyes. And if they still held back (Lily, worn out by the journey, fell asleep almost at once, but Mr. Carmichael read a book by candlelight)—if they still refused, saying that this splendor of his was mere vapor, that the dew was stronger than he was, and that they would rather sleep—then the voice would sing its song gently, without complaint or argument. The waves would break gently (Lily heard them as she slept); the light fell tenderly (it seemed to come to her through her eyelids). And it all looked, thought Mr. Carmichael, closing his book and drifting off, very much the way it had looked years ago.

before: She wanted to walk straight over and say, “Mr. Carmichael!” He would look up kindly, as he always did, out of his vague, smoky green eyes. But you only woke people when you knew what you wanted to tell them. And what she wanted to say was not one thing but everything. Small words that chopped the thought up into pieces said nothing at all. “About life, about death; about Mrs. Ramsay”—no, she thought, you could say nothing to anybody. The urgency of the moment always missed. Words fluttered off to the side and struck inches below the target. Then you gave up, and the idea sank back down, and you turned into what most middle-aged people become: cautious, secretive, with lines between the eyes and a look of permanent anxiety. Because how could you put these feelings of the body into words? How could you express that emptiness there? (She was looking at the drawing-room steps. They looked extraordinarily empty.) It was the body that felt it, not the mind. The physical sensations that came with the bare look of those steps had all at once turned extremely unpleasant. Wanting and not having sent a hardness, a hollowness, a strain right through her body. And then wanting and not having—wanting and wanting—how it wrung the heart, over and over! Oh, Mrs. Ramsay! she cried out without a sound, to that essence sitting by the boat, that abstraction made out of her, that woman in gray—as if to scold her for having gone, and then, having gone, for coming back. Thinking of her had seemed so safe. Ghost, air, nothing, something you could toy with easily and safely at any hour of the day or night—that was what she had been. And then suddenly she reached out her hand and wrung the heart like this. Suddenly the empty drawing-room steps, the frill of the chair inside, the puppy tumbling about on the terrace, the whole wave and whisper of the garden, turned into curves and arabesques flourishing around a center of total emptiness.

before: And now, little by little, the pain of wanting, and the bitter anger (at being called back just when she believed she would never grieve for Mrs. Ramsay again—had she missed her among the coffee cups at breakfast? Not at all), grew less. What their anguish left behind, as a remedy, was a relief that soothed in itself, and also, more mysteriously, a sense that someone was there—Mrs. Ramsay, freed for a moment of the weight the world had laid on her, lingering lightly beside Lily and then (for this was Mrs. Ramsay in all her beauty) lifting to her forehead a wreath of white flowers and going off with it. Lily squeezed her tubes again and attacked the problem of the hedge. It was odd how clearly she could see Mrs. Ramsay stepping, quick as always, across fields that were soft and purplish in their folds, full of flowers—hyacinths or lilies—among which she vanished. It was a trick of the painter’s eye. For days after hearing of her death, Lily had seen her like this, raising the wreath to her forehead and going off unquestioningly across the fields with her companion, a shadow. The sight, and the phrase, had power to comfort. Wherever she was—painting here in the country, or in London—the vision would come, and her eyes would half close, searching for something to rest the vision on. She would look down the railway carriage, or the bus; take a line from someone’s shoulder or cheek; look at the windows across the way; at Piccadilly strung with lamps at evening. All of it had been part of the fields of death. But there was always something—a face, perhaps, or a voice, or a newsboy calling _Standard, News_—that pushed through, snubbed her, woke her, and demanded, and in the end received, an effort of attention, so that the vision had to be made again and again. Now once more, driven by some instinctive need for distance and for blue, she gazed down at the bay, turning the blue bars of the waves into little hills and the more purple patches into stony fields. And once again, as always, something that didn’t belong startled her. In the middle of the bay was a brown speck. It was a boat—she saw that after a second. But whose? Mr. Ramsay’s, she answered. Mr. Ramsay: the man who had marched past her, aloof, with his hand raised, leading a procession, in those beautiful boots of his, asking for sympathy she had refused to give. By now the boat was halfway across the bay.

before: So this was the island, Cam thought, as she trailed her fingers through the waves again. Never before had she seen it from out at sea. So that was how it lay on the water: a dent in its middle, two sharp crags, the sea sweeping in there and stretching away for mile after mile on either side. It was tiny—shaped rather like a leaf standing on its end. So we took a little boat, she thought, and began telling herself an adventure story about escaping from a ship that was going down. But with the sea running through her fingers, and a sprig of seaweed disappearing behind them, she had no wish to tell herself a story in earnest. What she wanted was the feeling of adventure and escape. For as the boat sailed on she was thinking how everything had slipped away, passed, streamed off behind them: her father’s fury over the points of the compass, James’s obstinacy about their pact, her own misery. So what came next? Where were they heading? Out of her hand, icy cold, sunk deep in the sea, a fountain of joy shot up—joy at the change, the escape, the adventure (that she was alive, that she was here). And the drops from this sudden, thoughtless fountain fell here and there on the dark, drowsing shapes in her mind—shapes of a world she had not yet made real, turning in their darkness and catching a spark of light here and there: Greece, Rome, Constantinople. Tiny as it was, like a leaf on end, with the gold-flecked water flowing in and around it, did even that little island, she wondered, have its place in the universe? The old gentlemen in the study could have told her, she thought. Now and then she wandered in from the garden on purpose to catch them at it. There they would be (Mr. Carmichael, perhaps, or Mr. Bankes, very old and very stiff), facing each other in their low armchairs, crackling the pages of _The Times_ in front of them. She would come in from the garden with everything muddled in her head: something someone had said about Christ; a mammoth dug up in a London street; what had the great Napoleon been like? And they would take all this up in their clean hands (their clothes were gray; they smelled of heather), brush the scraps together, turn the paper, cross their knees, and every so often say something very short. As if in a trance, she would take a book off the shelf and stand watching her father write—so evenly, so neatly, from one edge of the page across to the other—coughing a little now and then, or saying something brief to the other old gentleman across from him. And standing there with her book open, she thought: here you could let any thought you had unfold like a leaf in water; and if it did well here, among the smoking old gentlemen and the crackle of _The Times_, then it was right. And as she watched her father writing in his study, she thought (sitting in the boat now) that he was utterly lovable and utterly wise; he was not vain, and he was no tyrant. Indeed, if he noticed her there with her book, he would ask her, as gently as anyone could, Was there nothing he could give her?

before: Some people must have disliked her intensely, Lily thought (Yes; she noticed the drawing-room step was empty, but it made no difference to her at all. She did not want Mrs. Ramsay now.)—people who found her too sure, too sweeping. Her beauty probably offended people as well. So monotonous, they would say—always the same! Their taste ran to another type, dark and vivacious. Then again, she was weak with her husband; she let him make those scenes of his. And she was reserved: nobody knew exactly what had happened to her. And (to return to Mr. Carmichael and his dislike) it was impossible to picture Mrs. Ramsay spending a whole morning on the lawn, standing at an easel or lying with a book. The idea was unthinkable. Saying nothing, with only the basket on her arm to show where she was going, she would set off for the town, to the poor, to sit in some airless little bedroom. How often Lily had watched her slip away without a word in the middle of a game or a discussion, basket on her arm, very upright. She had noticed when she came back. And she had thought, half laughing (she was so methodical about the teacups), half moved (her beauty took your breath away): eyes that are closing in pain have looked on you. You have been with them there.

before: During the War she had gone into a hall one day and heard him give a speech. He was denouncing something, condemning somebody. He was preaching brotherly love. And all she could feel was: how could he love humanity, this man who could not tell one picture from another—who had stood behind her smoking his shag (“fivepence an ounce, Miss Briscoe”) and made a point of telling her women can’t write, women can’t paint, not so much because he believed it as because, for some odd reason, he wanted it to be so? There he stood on a platform, lean and red and raucous, preaching love (among the plantains ants were crawling, and she disturbed them with her brush—red, busy ants, rather like Charles Tansley). From her seat in the half-empty hall she had watched him ironically as he pumped love into that cold space—and suddenly there was the old barrel, or whatever it had been, bobbing up and down in the waves, and Mrs. Ramsay hunting among the pebbles for her glasses case. “Oh dear! What a nuisance! Lost again. Don’t bother, Mr. Tansley. I lose thousands every summer.” At that he had pressed his chin back against his collar, as though afraid of seeming to approve such exaggeration—but he could put up with it from her, because he liked her—and had smiled very charmingly. He must have confided in her on one of those long excursions when people got separated and walked home alone. He was paying for his little sister’s education, Mrs. Ramsay had told her. It did him enormous credit. Her own picture of him was grotesque, Lily knew perfectly well, stirring the plantains with her brush. After all, half of what you thought about other people was grotesque. Such ideas served private purposes of your own. For her, he stood in for a whipping boy. When she was in a bad mood she caught herself flogging his lean flanks. If she wanted to take him seriously, she had to borrow Mrs. Ramsay’s sayings and see him through her eyes.

before: “Why don’t some of you take up botany? … With all those legs and arms why doesn’t one of you … ?” So they would chat, laughing, among the children, just as usual. Everything would be as usual—except for a kind of quiver, like a blade flashing in the air, that came and went between the two of them, as though the familiar sight of the children around their soup plates had been made new in their eyes by that hour among the pears and cabbages. Mrs. Ramsay, Lily thought, would look especially at Prue. Prue sat in the middle of her brothers and sisters, always so taken up, it seemed, with making sure nothing went wrong that she hardly said a word herself. How Prue must have blamed herself for that earwig in the milk! How pale she had turned when Mr. Ramsay flung his plate out of the window! How she wilted under those long silences between her parents! At any rate, her mother now seemed to be making it up to her—reassuring her that all was well, promising that some day that same happiness would be hers too. Yet she had had it for less than a year.

before: He read very fast, as though impatient to reach the end. And they really were very near the Lighthouse now. There it rose up, bare and upright, glaring black and white, and you could see the waves smashing into white splinters, like broken glass, against the rocks. You could make out lines and creases in the rock. You could see the windows plainly—one of them with a dab of white on it—and a little tuft of green on the rock. A man had come out, looked at them through a spyglass, and gone back in. So that was what it was like, James thought—the Lighthouse you had watched across the bay all these years: a bare tower standing on a naked rock. That satisfied him. It bore out some obscure feeling he had about his own nature. The old ladies, he thought, remembering the garden at home, went dragging their chairs about the lawn. Old Mrs. Beckwith, say, was forever going on about how nice it was, how sweet it was, how proud and how happy they all ought to be; but in actual fact, James thought, looking at the Lighthouse planted there on its rock, it’s like that. He looked at his father, reading fiercely, his legs tightly curled. The two of them shared that knowledge. “We are driving before a gale—we must sink,” he began murmuring to himself, half aloud, exactly the way his father said it.

You could make out lines and creases in the rock. You could see the windows plainly—one of them with a dab of white on it—and a little tuft of green on the rock. A man had come out, looked at them through a spyglass, and gone back in. So that was what it was like, James thought—the Lighthouse you had watched across the bay all these years: a bare tower standing on a naked rock. That satisfied him. It bore out some obscure feeling he had about his own nature. The old ladies, he thought, remembering the garden at home, went dragging their chairs about the lawn. Old Mrs. Beckwith, say, was forever going on about how nice it was, how sweet it was, how proud and how happy they all ought to be; but in actual fact, James thought, looking at the Lighthouse planted there on its rock, it’s like that. He looked at his father, reading fiercely, his legs tightly curled. The two of them shared that knowledge. “We are driving before a gale—we must sink,” James began murmuring to himself, half aloud, exactly the way his father said it.
